FROM MY DESK   Yesterday, the Treasury Department reported an eye-popping new milestone: U.S. gross debt surpassed $40 trillion. While economists view this threshold as largely symbolic, the sheer magnitude is hard to overstate, dwarfing the entire annual output of the U.S. economy. This morning, we look at how decades of higher spending on Medicare and social security, tax cuts and stimulus brought us here—and how a confluence of factors driving up bond yields just prompted Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent to step in as America’s “bond trader in chief.”

   This is an edition of The 10-Point newsletter, a guided tour of the best coverage in The Wall Street Journal. If you’re not subscribed, sign up here . If you’re reading this in your inbox, tap the headline above for online and audio versions of this newsletter. 

       2. TODAY’S HEADLINES   • Several women at defense contractor L3Harris Technologies shared concerns about CEO Chris Kubasik’s behavior years before his ouster .

   • The Army will phase out its new drone assault battalion , a unit established to bring U.S. troops up to speed on the latest cutting-edge military tech.

   • President Trump vowed to unleash what he called “ECONOMIC D-DAY” on Iran. His effort to squeeze Tehran into submission will depend heavily on curbing one of its biggest economic lifelines: Dubai.

   • The founder of Evergrande, the property giant that helped to spark a crisis in China’s real-estate sector, has been sentenced to life in prison for charges including fraud and financial misconduct.

   • Trump’s half-built White House ballroom puts the Supreme Court in a bind.

   • Six years after Prince Harry and his wife Meghan, Duchess of Sussex, quit royal duties and decamped to the U.S. West Coast, the family is planning to move back to the U.K.

   • The Stripe deal for OpenRouter, founded by an NFT entrepreneur, is a bet on a future where users turn to a mix of artificial-intelligence models.

   • To meet aggressive AI development timelines, big tech companies are cobbling together off-grid power systems —a workaround that comes with hefty price tags and operating risks, writes Jinjoo Lee.

       4. READ IT HERE FIRST   With tourism stalled, Hawaii chases the startup wave.   Kailua’s seaside streets bear the unmistakable look of a Hawaiian beach town, an oasis of palm trees, swimsuits and surfboards. Yet tucked behind a cafe where baristas make $11 lattes, young workers write code, design machinery and operate an industrial laser that can cut through a car door. Elsewhere on Oahu, students at the University of Hawaii make equipment bound for the moon. They are all part of a band of whip-smart engineers building an industry that officials hope will rescue Hawaii from a sagging tourism economy, depressed wages and an exodus of young residents to the mainland, reports Owen Tucker-Smith.

       5. REPORTER’S NOTEBOOK   Reporter Sara Ashley O’Brien: When I joined the Journal, in the fall of 2022, my first story looked at a little-known drug called Ozempic being injected by coastal elites to slim down. Interviewing people for that article, I learned they were experimenting with other injections—now widely known as peptides. Recently, I covered a dark side of GLP-1 usage: people seeking treatment for anorexia after taking medications like Ozempic and Mounjaro. I also reported on the young men ordering peptides online, injecting them without doctors’ supervision.

   These stories tend to arise from my observations: hearing a celebrity mention a drug or treatment on the red carpet, and then hearing it mentioned again on a podcast or in casual conversation in Los Angeles, where I live. Once I’ve heard about something in a few distinct places, I start to dig deeper.

   Wellness trends are driven by a collective desire for agency over the unpredictable. WSJ readers commonly ask me whether they should or shouldn’t try a particular supplement or treatment. It reveals that many are searching for an authority on something they’ve heard about, typically through social media or friends. People, by and large, want to live healthfully in an era when that feels increasingly difficult. After years of growth, the pipeline of 18-year-olds is dwindling because of lower birthrates. College enrollments are forecast to drop 13% by 2041, according to the Western Interstate Commission for Higher Education. According to PitchBook data, that record haul is nearly double California’s previous mark set in 2025 and more than triple the venture funding raised across the other 49 states combined. Despite concerns over a proposed state billionaire tax, massive investments in major AI companies continue to fuel the frenzy.

       9. AND FINALLY…   This 66-year-old overcame the odds and found a new job.   Lynn Lee had applied to hundreds of jobs after she was laid off from a soybean processing plant last year. She had become accustomed to being ignored or quickly dismissed by hiring managers. Like a lot of frustrated Americans, she had nearly given up. Her original story resonated with older job seekers. Reporter Sara Ashley O’Brien: When I joined the Journal, in the fall of 2022, my first story looked at a little-known drug called Ozempic being injected by coastal elites to slim down. 6. SEE THE STORY

 

America’s colleges are hurtling toward an enrollment cliff.

 
 
JOSH ULICK
 

Higher education is facing a falloff. After years of growth, the pipeline of 18-year-olds is dwindling because of lower birthrates. College enrollments are forecast to drop 13% by 2041, according to the Western Interstate Commission for Higher Education. Despite concerns over a proposed state billionaire tax, massive investments in major AI companies continue to fuel the frenzy.

 
 
 

9. AND FINALLY…

 

This 66-year-old overcame the odds and found a new job.

Finally, though, a breakthrough: This month, she started a new job.
